title: Find the weekday of any date in your head (the Doomsday rule)
description:
April 4, June 6, August 8, October 10 and December 12 always share a weekday, because each is exactly 63 days (9 weeks) after the last. John Conway called that weekday the year's doomsday (Saturday in 2026) and added landmarks for every month: 9/5 and 5/9, 7/11 and 11/7, Pi Day, and the last day of February. Doomsday moves one weekday a year and two into a leap year, so a year's doomsday is its century's anchor (Wednesday for the 1900s, Tuesday for the 2000s) plus the last two digits plus a quarter of them, minus whole weeks. This video covers why the dates line up, three ways to do the year step (including Conway's 'a dozen years is but a day' and the 2010 'odd + 11' method), why the century anchors are Tuesday, Sunday, Friday and Wednesday (400 years = 146,097 days = exactly 20,871 weeks), why the 13th falls on a Friday more often than any other day (688 times in 400 years), and what happened to the weekdays when Britain dropped 11 days in 1752.

Numbers checked in code: every date and count in the video against Python's calendar, all three year methods for every year 00-99 and every century 1800-2399, and the full mental method on 100,000 random dates (all correct). Sources: Wikipedia, Doomsday rule; Calendar (New Style) Act 1750.

beats.say: These five dates always fall on the same weekday. Every year.
By the end of this, you'll be able to name the weekday of any date from 1800 to 2199 in your head, in a few seconds. And you'll know why it works, which is the better part.
Start with the dates. April 4th, June 6th, August 8th, October 10th, December 12th. Four four, six six, eight eight, ten ten, twelve twelve.
This year, 2026, every one of them is a Saturday. Next year they'll all be Sundays. Whatever weekday they land on, they land on it together.
The mathematician John Conway called that shared weekday the year's doomsday. Once you know it, every month has a landmark you can count from.
Say you want Christmas. December 12th is a Saturday, so the 19th is, and the 26th. Christmas, the 25th, is one day before: a Friday.
That's the whole trick for this year. Two more steps, and it works for any year. But first, why should five random dates agree at all?
They aren't random. Count the days from April 4th to June 6th. 26 days left in April, 31 in May, and 6 in June. That's 63.
63 days is exactly 9 weeks. And the same thing happens from June 6th to August 8th, from August to October, and October to December. Every gap is 63 days. Nine weeks, on the nose.
So the even months are easy. The odd months need a phrase: I work 9 to 5 at the 7-Eleven.
That gives you May 9th and September 5th, and July 11th and November 7th. Nine five, five nine, seven eleven, eleven seven. All doomsdays.
March has one too. Pi Day, March 14th. It's three weeks before April 4th.
And January and February? February's last day is always a doomsday. In a normal year that's the 28th. In a leap year it's the 29th. And January has the 3rd in a normal year, the 4th in a leap year.
That's every month covered with a date you can remember. From now on, any date this year is just counting a few days from the nearest landmark.
If you like seeing the math inside everyday things, subscribe. There's a new one twice a day.
Now the real trick. Different years have different doomsdays. How do you find one without a calendar?
Watch what happens from one year to the next. A normal year is 365 days. That's 52 weeks and 1 day. So doomsday moves forward one weekday a year.
But if the new year has a February 29th, the extra day comes before its doomsday, so it jumps two. 2026 is Saturday, 2027 is Sunday, and 2028, a leap year, skips to Tuesday.
So for a year inside a century, count one step per year, plus one extra for every leap year. That's the last two digits, plus a quarter of them, rounded down.
Take 1969. The last two digits are 69. A quarter of 69, rounded down, is 17. 69 plus 17 is 86.
Now throw away whole weeks. 86 is 12 sevens, which is 84, with 2 left over. So 1969's doomsday is two days after the start of the century's doomsday.
The 1900s start on a Wednesday. Two days on: Friday. Doomsday in 1969 was a Friday.
Test it on something famous. Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20th, 1969. July's landmark is the 11th, a Friday. The 18th is a Friday too, so the 20th is a Sunday. It was.
If 69 plus 17 is too much arithmetic, Conway had a lazier version. He said a dozen years is but a day.
Twelve years is 4,383 days. That's 626 weeks and exactly 1 day. So every dozen years moves doomsday by one.
For 69: that's 5 dozens, with 9 left over. A quarter of 9 is 2. Add 5, 9 and 2: 16. Throw away two weeks: 2 again. Same answer, smaller numbers.
There's a third way, found in 2010, called odd plus 11. If the year is odd, add 11: 69 becomes 80. Halve it: 40. Count up to the next multiple of 7, which is 42: that's 2. No division by 4 at all.

Pick whichever sticks. They always agree. One more check: November 9th, 1989, the night the Berlin Wall opened. 89 plus 22 is 111, which leaves 6. Wednesday plus 6 is Tuesday. November 7th is a Tuesday, so the 9th was a Thursday. It was.
You've seen the 1900s start on a Wednesday. The 2000s start on a Tuesday. The 1800s, a Friday. The 2100s will start on a Sunday. Why those days?
Do the same counting across a whole century. Each of the 100 years moves doomsday one day, and each leap year moves it one more.
From 1900 to 2000 there are 25 leap years, because 2000 is one. 100 plus 25 is 125, which is 17 weeks and 6 days. Six days forward is one day back. Wednesday becomes Tuesday.
From 2000 to 2100 there are only 24, because 2100 won't be a leap year. 124 leaves 5. Five forward is two back. Tuesday becomes Sunday.
Keep going and the pattern is Tuesday, Sunday, Friday, Wednesday, and then Tuesday again in 2400. It repeats every 400 years.

That's not luck. 400 years of our calendar has 97 leap days, and 146,097 days in total. Divide by 7 and you get exactly 20,871 weeks. Not a single day left over. So the calendar of 2426 is the calendar of 2026, weekday for weekday.
So the four anchors are all you need. Tuesday for the 2000s, Wednesday for the 1900s, Friday for the 1800s, Sunday for the 2100s.
That 400-year cycle hides a strange fact. This month, November 13th was a Friday. It's the third Friday the 13th this year, after February and March.
Over one full 400-year cycle there are 4,800 thirteenths. If weekdays were shared out evenly, each would get about 686.
They aren't. Friday gets 688. Thursday and Saturday get only 684. The 13th lands on a Friday more often than on any other day of the week.
The cycle has a whole number of weeks, so the count never evens out. It's the same 688 every 400 years, forever. A small, fixed, slightly unlucky tilt.
You can check one more thing with doomsday. Every single year has at least one Friday the 13th, and never more than three.
There's one place the method needs care: old dates. Britain and its colonies used a different calendar until 1752.
The old one, the Julian calendar, had a leap day every four years with no exceptions. It drifted, and by 1752 it was 11 days behind.
So Parliament deleted them. In Britain, Wednesday, September 2nd, 1752 was followed by Thursday, September 14th.
The dates jumped 11, but the weekdays didn't skip. Wednesday was still followed by Thursday. Check it: the 1700s start on a Sunday, and doomsday says September 14th, 1752 was a Thursday.
So for any modern date, the method just works. For a date in Britain before 1752, or in much of Europe before 1582, you're on the old calendar, and you'd need its own anchors.
Conway worked this out in 1973, building on a method Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, had published. He could do it in under two seconds.
And he kept in practice. His computer was set up to quiz him on a random date every time he logged in.
Here's the full method once more. Find the century's anchor. Add the last two digits and a quarter of them. Throw away sevens. That's the year's doomsday.
Then jump to the month's landmark: four four, six six, eight eight, ten ten, twelve twelve, nine to five at the 7-Eleven, Pi Day, and the last day of February. Count to your date.

One more test. New Year's Day, 2000. The 2000s start on a Tuesday, and the last two digits are zero, so doomsday is Tuesday. 2000 is a leap year, so January's landmark is the 4th. Back three days: Saturday. It was.
We checked the whole method against a hundred thousand random dates between 1800 and 2199. It got every one right.
So here's yours. 2100 is not a leap year. What weekday will New Year's Day 2100 be? Put your answer in the comments, and the date you were born on, if you worked that out too.
